For N valid timesteps, gather histories/targets before scoring. Derived from the [original BPR-max objective](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/gru4rec_v2_cikm18.pdf), let p be positive scores and z negative scores: A=logsumexp(z), C=logsumexp(z+logsigmoid(p−z)); per-timestep loss is A−C, plus λ∑softmax(z)z² if enabled. Split K=128 into chunks; merge chunk A and C using torch.logaddexp. Never normalize softmax independently within chunks. Preserve the baseline’s epsilon convention: −log(exp(C−A)+ε) differs slightly from A−C.

Two exact implementation patterns: checkpoint each chunk’s embedding lookup and scoring, concatenate only N×K scores, then apply the global loss; or checkpoint chunk reductions and merge their logsumexp statistics. Negative embedding workspace becomes N×chunk_size×D. Plain Python chunking is insufficient: autograd can retain every chunk’s embeddings until backward. Use [checkpoint(..., use_reentrant=False)](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/checkpoint); pass fixed negative IDs explicitly and ensure recomputation uses identical inputs. Keep scores, normalization and softmax weights attached to autograd: detaching weights changes the objective’s gradients. Preserve score regularization with differentiable global normalization, preferably using retained N×K scores. These are implementation deductions, not benchmarked speed claims.

Verify against a dense reference using identical parameters, negative IDs, valid-position masks and reduction: compare scalar loss and gradients for features, embeddings, biases and GRU parameters. Use float64 [gradcheck](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/generated/torch.autograd.gradcheck.gradcheck.html), repeated negative IDs, extreme logits and uneven chunk boundaries; then check float32 tolerances. Measure peak CUDA memory and synchronized full-step runtime, including recomputation. Memory feasibility alone cannot establish feasibility within the fixed compute budget.
